records.name: Art-Reach Inc
records.summary: A nonprofit that helps disabled people take part in arts and culture. It offers an ACCESS Card that gets $2 admission at partner museums, theaters and gardens, runs free learning pages, and advises arts groups on access.
records.what_you_do: Register for an ACCESS Card to pay $2 admission at partner arts sites, read the free Community Learning pages, or sign up for paid accessibility workshops made for arts staff. Arts groups can also ask for accessibility training or consulting.

cost.text: The ACCESS Card gives $2 admission at partner sites. Eligible people are those with a qualifying state ACCESS or EBT card, and people with disabilities who buy an Art-Reach ACCESS Card. The page does not give the card's own price.

first_step.how: Register for an ACCESS Card through the purchase link on art-reach.org. The free Community Learning content does not mention any sign up.
first_step.basis: Anyone who qualifies can get the card through a public online form, and the free learning content is open to all. The page does not describe a group or class to try first.
first_step.what_to_expect: The ACCESS Card gets $2 admission at partner museums, theaters and gardens. Art-Reach is an organization rather than a group that meets, so a first step is usually online: the card form, the newsletter, or a free learning page. The page does not say how the card is shown at the door.
first_visit_tips: Check art-reach.org for current partner sites before you go, since the site gives different counts on different pages.
If you qualify through a state ACCESS or EBT card, bring that card with you.

records.notes: Partner site counts differ: the homepage says more than 100 sites and the programs page says over 80, so the record gives no count. The homepage copyright line reads 2023 and is not used as evidence. Accessibility Basics is a six-part arts staff series on Zoom with ASL interpretation and captions, $25 a session or $100 for all six, with a free local offer on the page that is not recorded here; the first session is October 13, 2026 and the rest run into 2027. STAMP (free museum visits for Philadelphia high school students with a student ID) is also an Art-Reach program and is not a separate record. The card and newsletter forms are hosted on a third-party form service. No dated webinar or event was found, so status is probably_active.

records.name: ArtWell Collaborative
records.summary: A Philadelphia nonprofit that helps young people make art and poetry. Its work runs through school and library programs such as We the Poets, EcoArts and student art shows, and its public workshops, family days and poetry and art show are listed on its events page.
records.what_you_do: Email the program director through the Get Involved page to volunteer in development, design, finance or community engagement, go to a public workshop or family day from the events page, or apply to the board through the Join the Board page. Schools and groups can request a youth program or pop up workshop through a form.

schedule.text: Public workshops, skill builds, family days and the poetry and art show are posted on the events page with their own dates. Student programs run in schools and libraries on dates each host sets. The poetry and art show is held in May at The Galleries at Moore College of Art and Design.

locations.label: Galleries at Moore College of Art and Design (poetry and art show)

cost.text: Public workshops, family days and volunteering are free where listed. Youth programs are fee based for agencies outside its core partner network, though grant sponsored workshops are sometimes available.

first_step.how: Watch the events page for a public workshop or family day, then go. To volunteer, email the program director listed on the Get Involved page.
first_step.basis: Public events are listed with dates and times, and the volunteer roles name a contact to write to. The event listings do not say whether you must sign up before you attend.
first_step.what_to_expect: Public skill builds have usually run about two hours on a Saturday afternoon, with hands-on poetry, art or self-care sessions. Lunch and learn talks run about an hour and are often online. Family days run most of the day, and the events page does not say how many people attend.
first_visit_tips: Open the event's own page for the exact address, since past events were held at the ArtWell office on West Oxford Street and at partner venues.
For a school or youth group, use the Request a Program form on the site or call 215-220-6253.
Ask the program director by email before you come to volunteer for the first time.

records.notes: Correction to tier 1: the October 4, 2026 family day is in the past (the events page lists it at the Barnes Foundation, 10 am to 4 pm), and the page lists no later family day, so it is not 'still upcoming'. Other 2026 listings are a September 19, 2026 pop up workshop at Please Touch Museum and a February 25, 2026 lunch and learn. The poetry and art show page gives a Sunday, May 23 opening with no year, so it is not dated. The board page asks for four to five mostly virtual meetings a year, a term of at least two years, and a meaningful gift. Youth program fees and locations are not published. Partner groups named on the youth programs page are listed as leads.

records.name: ARTZ Philadelphia
records.summary: A nonprofit that brings arts programs to people living with dementia and their care partners. Programs include museum conversations, music and art sessions, and caregiver cafes, held online and in person.
records.what_you_do: Join a program as a person living with dementia or as a care partner, or go to a public event such as an ARTZ at The Museum visit. Volunteers help with phone reminders, tech support calls, blog posts, event help and kit assembly after a training session, and the organization also has a board you can join.

schedule.text: Programs run online and in person across the Philadelphia area. ARTZ at The Museum meets weekly at museums and art centers for about an hour each. The Side by Side pilot for care pairs meets monthly.

cost.text: Public programs are free to join, according to the program FAQ. Event listings also show free admission.

first_step.how: Pick a program on the Participate page, then register on its event page. For programs set up by arrangement, email info@artzphilly.org.
first_step.basis: The FAQ says you can join one program at a time and drop in or out, and the site explains how to start and welcomes people who are new. Event listings still say registration is required, so register ahead.
first_step.what_to_expect: Most programs last about an hour. Groups are small, about 6 to 8 people online and 15 to 16 in person, led by a trained facilitator, and the talk is mostly conversation, sometimes with hands-on art or music making. You can take part as much or as little as you like.
first_visit_tips: Register on the event page first, because the event listings ask for it.
Check whether the session is online (Zoom) or in person, since in-person event pages give the venue address and transit notes.
Note any needs on the questionnaire that new participants fill in, or email info@artzphilly.org.
Ask whether masks are recommended before an indoor session, since the FAQ's mask advice may be out of date.

access.notes: The organization says it makes every effort to accommodate special needs. New participants can list specific needs on a questionnaire, and in-person event pages include transit information for each venue.

records.notes: The FAQ says public programs are free and that people can drop in, while the October 2026 event listings say registration is required; the record shows both and asks people to register. The FAQ's mask advice refers to a past COVID surge. Listed October 2026 sessions include ARTZ at The Museum visits at Woodmere, the Barnes Foundation and Main Line Art Center, and Side by Side sessions at Center in the Park and KleinLife. The 2026 Gala on November 5, 2026 is a fundraiser, not a program. Cost, accessibility of venues and the volunteer form itself were not fully readable. Venue museums are not listed as leads.

records.name: ASAP Scrabble Clubs
records.summary: The Scrabble program of ASAP, a Philadelphia nonprofit for after-school and summer activities. Students play Scrabble each week in school, library and rec center clubs, take part in citywide events, and can join a school league that runs from November to February.
records.what_you_do: Students join a weekly Scrabble club at a school, library or rec center and play in citywide events. Students in grades 3 to 12 can compete in pairs, and early readers in grades K to 2 can take part in events such as read alouds and Scrabble SLAM.

schedule.text: Weekly club play in schools, libraries and rec centers. Days and times vary by club and are not listed on ASAP's pages. The Philadelphia Scholastic Scrabble League runs from November through February.

locations.label: Partner schools, libraries and rec centers citywide

cost.text: No student fee is listed on ASAP's Scrabble pages. Partner sites can talk with ASAP about sharing costs through a cost sharing agreement.

first_step.how: Find a club on ASAP's program locator at phillyasap.org/asap-directory/, or email scrabble@phillyasap.org to ask about joining.
first_step.basis: Youth and parents in Philadelphia are invited to find a club on the locator or to email the program. The pages do not say whether a club has open seats.
first_step.what_to_expect: Club members play Scrabble with other students once a week in a school or library, using boards and materials ASAP supplies to the site. The league plays matches from November to February, and elementary and middle school teams get rides to after school matches. The pages do not say how long a club session lasts.
first_visit_tips: Ask the club leader or site staff when and where the club meets, since ASAP's pages do not list those.
Ask whether the club is taking new players this season.

records.notes: Name kept from tier 1. ASAP runs chess, debate, drama and Scrabble; this record covers Scrabble only. The contact email from tier 1 (chess@) is replaced by the Scrabble address on the Scrabble page. The only dated item behind status is a January 2026 news story about ASAP's chess tournament, and no dated Scrabble item was found, so re-check status when the 2026 to 2027 league posts. Figures conflict: the Scrabble page says more than 1,100 students in 85 clubs and the programs page says 1,500 students in 80 clubs. The start a club page says club leaders must be able to get clearances to work with youth; that is for site leaders, not students, so it is not in requirements. A search snippet (not read as a page) showed a league match listed for December 18, 2025 at 440 N. Broad St.; not used in the record.

records.name: Asian Americans United
records.summary: A Philadelphia nonprofit, founded in 1985, that builds leadership in Asian American communities. It runs youth leadership programs, a yearly Mid-Autumn Festival in Chinatown, culture and storytelling projects, and civic and immigrant rights work.
records.what_you_do: Sign up for the volunteer form on the Get Involved page, help run activities at the Mid-Autumn Festival, ask by email about its Youth Leadership Development Programs, or join its civic and immigrant rights work. Friends can also sign up for the newsletter or give through the site.

schedule.text: The Mid-Autumn Festival is one of two major events each year, with the other an anniversary celebration. Youth program schedules are not published on the pages read.

locations.label: Mid-Autumn Festival street site in Chinatown (10th Street closed to traffic)

cost.text: The festival page does not say whether it is free or ticketed. Youth program costs are not listed.

first_step.how: Go to the Mid-Autumn Festival in Chinatown on the date on its festival page (check first, since the stage schedule may change), or sign up on the volunteer form linked from the Get Involved page.
first_step.basis: It is a public, family friendly street festival, and the site gives a volunteer form and an email address. Youth leadership deadlines and steps are not listed on the pages read.
first_step.what_to_expect: The main stage runs from noon into the evening, and the festival ends with a lantern parade. Visitors can make lanterns or try calligraphy and carnival games, watch performances such as lion dances and dance groups, and eat from local restaurants. The page describes it as drawing thousands of families.
first_visit_tips: Check the festival page for the latest date and stage times before you go.
Plan for most of an afternoon if you want to see the parade at the end.
Look up transit or parking separately, since the page does not describe either.

records.notes: The festival page gives October 3 with headings that say 2026, but no year is printed beside the date, and it warns the main stage schedule may change because of a new date. Check the page before any visit. The events page lists no dated events and points people to social media. The youth leadership link returned HTTP 404 when tried, so youth program details are not verified beyond the Get Involved page menu. Festival performing groups are not named in full, so none are listed as leads.

records.name: Asian Arts Initiative
records.summary: An arts center on Vine Street with a free gallery, exhibitions, performances and community nights. It also runs youth arts programs for middle and high school students, and takes volunteer sign ups and gallery tour requests through forms on its site.
records.what_you_do: Visit the free gallery on a Thursday, Friday or Saturday afternoon, buy a ticket to a performance or community night, request a gallery tour or volunteer through the forms on the site, or ask about the Youth Arts Workshop or the Youth Leadership Initiative.

schedule.text: The gallery is open Thursday to Saturday, 2 to 6 pm. Performances and events run on their own dates, listed on the site.

cost.text: Gallery admission is always free. Performance and event prices vary by event, and tickets are sold through the site.

access.notes: The page says the building is mobility accessible, with access to all public floors and spaces. Each floor has single occupant, non-gendered restrooms with a changing station, and seating accommodations are available at programmed events. If you contact the group in advance, it will try to meet requests such as assistive technology or materials in another format. A fragrance free space is not guaranteed because most events are open to the public.

first_step.how: Visit the gallery on a Thursday, Friday or Saturday between 2 and 6 pm, when entry is free. For a youth program, use the email or interest form linked from the Get Involved page.
first_step.basis: The gallery is open to walk in visitors during posted hours, and events are sold to the public. The youth programs take inquiries by email or an interest form, but the enrollment steps are not spelled out.
first_step.what_to_expect: A gallery visit is free and open during posted afternoon hours, with exhibitions to walk through. The building is described as mobility accessible, with restrooms on every floor. Performances and community nights need a ticket, and seating is set up for programmed events.
first_visit_tips: Use the map link on the Visit page to plan your route, since the site does not describe the entrance.
If you need an accommodation, contact the group in advance using the address on the Visit page.
If fragrances bother you, mention it ahead of time, since a fragrance free space is not guaranteed.

records.notes: Corrections to tier 1: the schedule and cost text had dated events (Careoke Club, Artist Town Hall) which now sit outside the record text. The Youth Leadership Initiative is for grades 9 to 12, free, with fall and spring semesters, a four week summer camp, and an email inquiry; the Youth Arts Workshop is for middle school students, runs year round with summer and after school sessions, had summer 2026 registration open, and links a 2026 to 2027 interest form; its cost is not stated. Camp Bruce Lee is listed under education but was not read. The footer phone number differs from the one on the Visit page, so check before calling. The Careoke night (October 9, 2026, $15 to $25 through Eventbrite, under 18 free with a caregiver) is the newest dated evidence.

records.name: Association for Public Art
records.summary: A Philadelphia organization that runs public art projects, including Art on the Parkway, and keeps a public art map and a digital archive of public art from 1872 to 1980.
records.what_you_do: See public artworks on view outdoors, such as Let Freedom Ring at Cherry Street Pier and Franklin Thread in Maja Park, join a walking tour, talk or family day from the events page, or browse the public art map and archive. The pages read do not describe class or volunteer roles.

schedule.text: Walking tours, talks and family days run as a series on posted dates, listed on the events page. Public artworks stay on view outdoors for set periods.

locations.label: Cherry Street Pier (Let Freedom Ring), Race Street and Columbus Boulevard

cost.text: Event costs are not listed on the events page, and the artwork page does not say whether viewing is free.

first_step.how: See Let Freedom Ring at Cherry Street Pier, on view through November 1, 2026, or open a walking tour's own event page from the events page for its time, meeting place and cost.
first_step.basis: The outdoor artworks are public, and each event has its own page. The events list does not show sign up steps, so check each event page to see whether you need to register.
first_step.what_to_expect: Public artworks are outdoors, so a visit is a walk to the site, with the artwork page listing Friday to Sunday hours from 2 to 8 pm for Let Freedom Ring. Walking tours, talks and family days appear on the events page, and each links to its own page with the details. The events list does not say how many people attend.
first_visit_tips: Open the public art map to find artworks, then open each artwork's own page for its dates and site.
Check each event page for the start time and meeting spot, since the events list shows only dates.

records.notes: The events page lists 2026 items from April through a walking tour on October 17, 2026, including artist talks, walking tours and a family day, but the list gives no times, places, costs or registration method, so each event page is needed. Let Freedom Ring is on view June 4 to November 1, 2026 per its artwork page, and Franklin Thread is listed through October 2026 on the homepage. The public art map page does not say whether it is free and showed no artworks in the captured version. Class and volunteer roles were not found. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Marian Anderson Historical Society appear as partners on event listings and are listed as leads.
